narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Ōte'a predates European contact in Tahiti, originally serving as a male-only dance.
It was documented in 1928 by Teuira Henry as a violent, jerky war dance.
The modern form was established in the second half of the 20th century through the Heiva i Tahiti festival.
on_screen: Map: French Polynesia · Oceania
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a central feature of Tahitian cultural identity and is performed at festivals like the Heiva i Tahiti.
It serves as a narrative medium, with gestures reenacting daily occupations, nature, or historical themes.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers stand in rows and perform synchronized movements.
Women focus on hip-shaking (fa'arapu), while men perform scissor-like leg movements (pa'oti).
The dance includes 23 regulated steps for men in competition.
Watch for fa'arapu, pa'oti.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (2QahgraRrYs)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers in several rows
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is strictly percussion-based, featuring the tōʻere (slit log), the pahu (shark-skin drum), and the faʻatētē.
There is no singing.
Listen for the tōʻere, pahu, faʻatētē.
A rapid, driving sound produced by wooden slit drums and skin-covered drums, characterized by complex, interlocking rhythmic patterns without melodic accompaniment.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes typically include plant-fiber skirts (more), headpieces, and necklaces.
Tassels are used to accentuate hip movement.
Modern versions may use synthetic materials like polyester or reflective surfaces.
on_screen: Images — MISSING
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: The dance is performed in three forms: Ōte'a tāne (men), Ōte'a vahine (women), and Ōte'a ʻāmui (mixed).
It is a form of 'ori tahiti, sharing roots with other traditional Tahitian dances, though distinct from the melodic aparima.

scenes.title: Family tree
